extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP counsel, and corporate clients concerned with U.S. §101 patent eligibility (especially for computer-implemented inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the Supreme Court's Alice/Mayo two-step framework to determine whether claimed inventions—particularly computer-implemented inventions—are patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Focuses on identifying abstract ideas and whether additional claim elements supply an 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A]ny new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof" is eligible for patent protection under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that § 101 defines the statutory categories of patentable subject matter, but that judicial exceptions exist (laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas). The § 101 inquiry serves to prevent monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work that would impede innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to § 101 (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicially-created exception exists where the claimed invention is (1) a law of nature; (2) a natural phenomenon; or (3) an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the policy rationale: these exceptions prevent patents from monopolizing foundational tools. Also note the caveat that virtually all inventions embody or apply such concepts at some level, so the exception requires careful application (citing Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step Alice/Mayo framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court uses a two-step framework: first determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); second, determine whether the claim elements contain an "inventive concept" sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply step 1 to identify whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea; if so, apply step 2 to examine whether elements add something significantly more than the abstract idea itself. Both steps are required to resolve § 101 eligibility under Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — determine if claims are directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step of the eligibility inquiry is to determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict 'abstract ideas' only to 'preexisting, fundamental truth[s] that exist in principle apart from any human action'—economic practices like risk hedging or intermediated settlement can be 'abstract ideas.' Use precedent (e.g., Bilski) and analyze whether the claimed concept is a longstanding building block of commerce or technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — look for an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claims are directed to an abstract idea, assess whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating an abstract idea and adding the words 'apply it' is not enough. Limiting the use of an abstract idea to a particular technical environment is also insufficient absent additional inventive concept. The inquiry focuses on whether the additional elements do more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not render an abstract idea patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not transform that abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that requires a 'substantial and meaningful role for the computer' is not necessarily patent eligible; the Court focuses on the type of use of the computer. If the computer is performing 'well-understood, routine, conventional activit[ies]' previously known to the industry, those computer limitations do not 'transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of specific or conventional hardware cannot save an otherwise ineligible claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting particular hardware or a system with specific hardware cannot save a claim that is otherwise ineligible where the hardware does not offer a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the use of the method to a particular technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether hardware elements add anything 'meaningful' beyond conventional implementation; mere linking to a technological environment is insufficient under Alice (slip op., at 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of claim types and software/algorithm novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-implemented inventions—especially those whose novelty lies in an algorithm implemented through software—remain vulnerable to § 101 attack; method and computer-readable medium claims were found ineligible in Alice, and system claims are not necessarily immune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that litigation will focus on whether the claimed invention is based on an 'abstract idea' and whether claims contain inventive concept beyond conventional computation. There is a judicial preference for dedicated physical elements over purely software implementations; non-practicing entities' business-model-style patents are particularly at risk.
